source: Identity fields follow IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) and NIST isotopic compositions, vendored for offline play. Each element fact has its own source.

elements.name: Hydrogen
elements.fact: The lightest element. Stars are mostly hydrogen, and every water molecule carries two hydrogen atoms.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Helium
elements.fact: A noble gas. Helium gas is less dense than air, so a balloon of it rises. It almost never bonds with other atoms.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Lithium
elements.fact: A soft, light metal used in phone and laptop batteries.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Beryllium
elements.fact: A stiff, light metal used in some aerospace parts. The mineral beryl contains it.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Boron
elements.fact: A metalloid. Borax cleaners and some heat-resistant glass contain boron.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Carbon
elements.fact: Diamonds, pencil graphite, and every living thing are built on carbon.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Nitrogen
elements.fact: About 78% of the air you breathe is nitrogen gas, N₂.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Oxygen
elements.fact: You breathe O₂. Oxygen is also locked inside the rocks of Earth's crust.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
elements.note: The grade-level Lewis model of O2 is a double bond. Molecular orbital theory, beyond this course, explains why oxygen gas is paramagnetic. The stored weight 15.9994 lies inside the CIAAW interval; many textbooks round it to 15.999.

elements.name: Fluorine
elements.fact: The most reactive halogen. Fluoride compounds help protect tooth enamel.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Neon
elements.fact: A noble gas. True neon glows red-orange inside glass tubes.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
elements.note: Pure neon discharge glows red-orange. Other sign colors use different gases or phosphors.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.fact: A soft metal that reacts with water. Table salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Magnesium
elements.fact: Burns with a brilliant white light. A magnesium ion sits at the center of chlorophyll.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Aluminum
elements.fact: A light metal used for drink cans and airplanes. It does not rust the way iron does.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
elements.note: US textbook spelling is aluminum. The IUPAC spelling is aluminium. Drink-can sheet is an aluminum alloy, not pure Al.

elements.name: Silicon
elements.fact: Computer chips are made from silicon. Quartz sand, common on many beaches, is silicon dioxide.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
elements.note: Quartz is SiO2. Many continental beaches are quartz sand; many tropical beaches are calcium carbonate instead.

elements.name: Phosphorus
elements.fact: Part of DNA and of the ATP molecules your cells use for energy.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Sulfur
elements.fact: A yellow solid. Some of its compounds smell like rotten eggs, and it is used to toughen rubber.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Chlorine
elements.fact: A halogen. Chlorine compounds keep pool water clean, and with sodium they make table salt.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Argon
elements.fact: The third most common gas in air. Some light bulbs are filled with argon so the filament lasts longer.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.fact: An alkali metal your nerves and muscles need. Potatoes, beans, yogurt, and bananas all contain it.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Calcium
elements.fact: Bones and teeth store most of the calcium in your body, inside compounds. Limestone and seashells are calcium compounds too.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Scandium
elements.fact: A rare transition metal sometimes added to aluminum to make it stronger.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Titanium
elements.fact: Strong, light, and used in some bone implants because the body tolerates it well.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.fact: Added to steel to make it tougher. Some sea squirts concentrate vanadium from seawater.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Chromium
elements.fact: Mixed into stainless steel, where it helps the surface resist rust.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Manganese
elements.fact: A transition metal used in steelmaking. Your body needs a tiny amount of it.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Iron
elements.fact: Iron ions in hemoglobin carry oxygen in your blood. Most of the steel in buildings is iron.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Cobalt
elements.fact: A blue color in some glass and glazes comes from cobalt. It is also used in many batteries.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Nickel
elements.fact: A tough metal used in coins and in stainless steel.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Copper
elements.fact: Copper wires carry electricity into homes. The Statue of Liberty is covered in copper that turned green.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Zinc
elements.fact: Galvanized nails are coated in zinc so the iron underneath rusts more slowly.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Gallium
elements.fact: A metal that can melt in your hand. It melts at about 30 °C, just above room temperature.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
elements.note: Gallium's melting point is 29.7646 °C, so a sample can melt from the warmth of a hand.

elements.name: Germanium
elements.fact: A metalloid used in some infrared lenses and older electronics.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Arsenic
elements.fact: A metalloid that is toxic in many of its compounds. Tiny controlled amounts are used in some electronics.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Selenium
elements.fact: Your body needs a tiny amount. Selenium colors some glass, and older photocopiers used it to capture an image.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Bromine
elements.fact: The only halogen that is a liquid at room temperature. It is a deep red-brown.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Krypton
elements.fact: A noble gas used in some bright flashes and camera lights. It is not the fictional mineral.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Silver
elements.fact: Silver conducts electricity better than any other metal. Everyday wires are usually copper. Old photographs used silver compounds to capture light.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Iodine
elements.fact: A gray-purple halogen your body needs in tiny amounts. Iodized salt adds an iodine compound, not crystals of the element.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.

elements.name: Gold
elements.fact: Gold barely reacts with air or water, which is why ancient gold jewelry still shines.
elements.source: IUPAC CIAAW Standard Atomic Weights (2024) for atomic number, symbol, group, period, and atomic weight; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for the most abundant isotope. Fact checked against OpenStax Chemistry 2e.
